headline: A month in a city canal. Busan's shark is free.
summary: A three-metre female shark swam into a canal in Busan, South Korea, last month and could not get back out. Locals named her Bukangi, and huge crowds came to the water's edge to watch. Unusually warm water and plenty of fish may have drawn her in. Officials used nets to guide her toward the sea, and AP News reports she is out.

cover_question.q: Why did it take a month?

cover_answer: Nets and at least three tries. The BBC doesn't say why.
table_question: A wild animal wanders into town. Help it out, or leave it be?

5-7.script: A shark as long as a car swam into a canal in a city in South Korea and couldn't find her way back out. She stayed a whole month, and people gave her a name, Bukangi. Big crowds came to the edge to look at her. Helpers used long nets to steer her back to the sea, and now she is out.
5-7.why: A shark as long as a car, a crowd, a net, and out. The ending comes in the first telling.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them and takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script hands them a shark as long as a car, a crowd at the water's edge and a net, with the ending in the first telling. Nothing dies. Expect "can a shark come in our pool?" No. She needs the sea, and now she has it.

8-12.script: Last month a three-metre shark turned up in a canal in Busan, South Korea. The water was unusually warm and full of fish, so she may have followed dinner in and stayed. Nets laid out like cones steering traffic pointed her back at the sea. At least three tries, huge crowds, and now she is out.
8-12.why: Warm water, fish, a wrong turn, a net. Cones are the mechanism.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect, so the script runs one chain: warm water, plenty of fish, a shark that follows them in and stays. Nets as traffic cones is a mechanism they know, steering rather than grabbing. Expect "why didn't they just catch her?" Guiding, not catching, is the method, and it took several goes.

13-17.script: Why did it take a month to get her out? Officials in Busan tried nets at least three times to guide a three-metre shark back to the sea while crowds lined the canal. Second: the BBC says unusually warm water may have drawn her in. If the sea keeps warming, is this a one-off or the first of many?
13-17.why: A slow rescue and a warm sea. Let them connect the two, or not.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can reason about what is not in front of them, so the script hands them the one detail that points past the canal: the water was unusually warm. They can hold the rescue and its cause together and decide whether the cause worries them. Expect "is that climate change?" The BBC doesn't say, and the question is fair.

5-7.a: Maybe. She was in a strange place for a month. Now she is back in the sea where she belongs.

8-12.q: Why did she go into the canal?
8-12.a: Warm water and plenty of fish may have drawn her in, the BBC says.

8-12.q: How do you move a shark?
8-12.a: With nets, to steer her toward the sea. It took at least three tries.

13-17.q: Why did it take a month?
13-17.a: Nets and at least three tries. The BBC doesn't say why.

13-17.q: Is warm water a sign of something bigger?
13-17.a: The BBC says the water was unusually warm and stops there. Fair to wonder.
